experiments.title: World open: backdrop built once, shape measurements cached
experiments.hypothesis: Opening a world (every door) built the web backdrop twice (the load, then the host's fit) and re-measured every part of every actor (SVG path parsing) and re-asked per-blueprint questions (size class, clean-up families) on every load.
experiments.method: Web rail world-open (load to two painted frames), 8 worlds x low/mid throttle, median of 3 interleaved rounds against the develop demo build; node A/B of 17 warm-kit world loads interleaved x5; profiles (Chromium CPU at 6x, node --cpu-prof); scene fingerprint over all 561 worlds x 2 sizes; backdrop pixel compare after open, door and back.
experiments.before: web world-open total low 12362 ms / mid 6687 ms (8 worlds); node warm load sum 40.5 ms (17 worlds), worst 3.59 ms; kit build 245 ms
experiments.after: low 8731 ms (-29%) / mid 4550 ms (-32%), every world faster (19-43%); node sum 26.3 ms (-35%), worst 2.58 ms; kit build 175 ms. Re-measured after rebasing on develop db61cd17 (EXP-033 static underlay): low 12604 -> 8703 ms (-30.9 %), mid 6813 -> 4533 ms (-33.5 %), every world -26..-42 % (results/EXP-034/*-rebased.json)
experiments.evidence: 1122 scenes identical (6740 dirt spots); backdrop pixels identical (36 states); worldOpen.webdom.test (red without the guard or the scenery mark); record-open veh-roads 2488 -> 1550 ms, playground 1216 -> 980 ms at 6x. DOM nodes after idle read higher (veh-roads 10594 -> 12588): every extra node is inside the scenery raster-tile images (removing the tile <image>s leaves 6511 vs 6529). On develop the second, redundant backdrop build discarded the tiles before the ones under the camera were rasterised (only tile 0 of veh-roads ever became an image), so the visible scenery stayed live vectors repainted every frame; now the tiles in view rasterise as designed, which is also why idle dropped frames fell (low veh-harbour 11.43 -> 4.81 %).. On the rebased tree: viewport pixels of the stage (cast, effects and the area banner hidden) identical in 20/24 states; the other 4 differ by 8-71 px on wave/hill edges at a raster-tile boundary (tile image vs live vectors) and the sun glow, the same order as a same-build control (8 and 34 px).

experiments.title: Web: the moving layers drawn on a canvas by the native Skia renderer (renderer 'auto')
experiments.hypothesis: after EXP-033 the moving cast is ~half of a low-end frame's paint: every frame the browser re-records and re-rasterises the svg of every visible object; drawing them on one canvas with the SkiaStageRenderer native already ships removes that
experiments.method: CanvasStage + 2D-canvas Skia adapter (own transform stack), hit test = the drawing replayed (isPointInPath) in DOM order; canvas-parity.mjs + canvas-hit-parity.mjs on frozen frames; e2e suite in both renderers; web-trace interleaved (software compositing); web-bench low+mid interleaved x2 with --gpu (GPU raster + compositing on SwiftShader)
experiments.before: svg: software-compositing traces paint 1.1-1.2 s per low-end playground drag; GPU path (--gpu) dropped-sum 4 335 over 24 cells x 2 runs, input-p95-sum 9 580 ms
experiments.after: canvas: software path paint -65 %, rAF JS equal, but compositor commit +0.6-0.7 s (each canvas frame copied on the main thread): drag RunTask -8..10 %, idle worse. GPU path: dropped-sum 1 894 (-56 %), input-p95-sum 6 233 ms (-35 %); e.g. low playground drag-hold 99.7/99.9 -> 15/20 %, tap-spam (mid) 100/100 -> 19/18 %, low market drag-fast 95/95 -> 25/18 %; swipe small gains. Parity: <= 0.6 % px differ > 24/255 (edge AA); hit actor >= 99.95 %, part >= 99.67 %; e2e identical in both renderers
experiments.decision: kept (renderer 'auto' default: canvas where the browser composites on a GPU, svg under software compositing / software GL)
experiments.evidence: results/EXP-035/*. On GPU-less runners the GPU path is emulated on the same CPU (SwiftShader): svg's per-frame raster competes for CPU, so the GPU-path magnitude is likely overstated vs real phone GPUs; direction agrees with the software-path paint -65 %. Not verified on a real device. Native renderer unchanged except opt-in options; native still draws a part that precedes its parent in z order nested (ostrich tuft over head) unlike the web

experiments.title: Rig: riders carried by their host's bones (cost measured, no action)
experiments.hypothesis: The rig pass (every rider's world transform composed from its host's bone each frame, plus Skia's per-rider SVD decompose) could cost real frame time once every carrier in a world is loaded and driven.
experiments.method: perf-rig.ts (new): every carrier loaded (2 riders each where possible), carriers driven by pointer for 600 frames while the others are tapped; per frame: engine tick, the rig pass alone (Rig.apply wrapped), Skia draw; same world unloaded as baseline; 15 worlds (vehicle, haul, construction, farm, harbor).
experiments.before: unloaded worlds: frame p95 0.8-2.6 ms
experiments.after: loaded worlds: rig pass p95 0.017-0.135 ms per frame; frame p95 0.8-3.1 ms; loaded vs unloaded within run-to-run noise
experiments.evidence: results/EXP-036/rig-*.json (perf-rig output). The only frame drops in the run were door frames, unrelated to the rig: see EXP-037. Not verified on a device: CanvasKit on a 4-vCPU VM.

experiments.title: Engine: interaction-rule lookup indexed by actor selector (door frame 218 ms → 11 ms)
experiments.hypothesis: A 50-324 ms tick spike when a door opens (in loaded and unloaded worlds alike) is not the rig: the scene load asks ruleFor for every pair of the new cast (hasSnapKit), and ruleFor scanned all ~4 400 interaction rules per new pair.
experiments.method: perf-rig worst-frame report (spike at the door frame f75-f96 in both arms); in-process CPU profile of the door frame (ruleFor ~210 ms of a 218 ms tick); fix: rules indexed by actor selector (blueprint id or #tag), merged in original order, built once; ruleIndex.test compares against the first-match scan over 9k+ pairs and keeps rule order (red when the merge order is reversed); perf-engine over all 561 worlds after.
experiments.before: door frame (veh-railway) tick 218 ms; worst frame over 15 worlds 324 ms (haul-farm)
experiments.after: door frame 11 ms (16.7 ms with the profiler attached); worst frame over 15 worlds 39 ms; all 561 worlds: mean tick 73 µs, worst p95 0.69 ms, worst load 17 ms
experiments.evidence: ruleIndex.test.ts (red with reversed merge order); results: rig before/after, engine over 561 worlds. Absolute numbers from a 4-vCPU VM; compare within the run.

experiments.title: Door: the scene load and the new scene's first draw on separate frames
experiments.hypothesis: After EXP-037 the door frame still paid the scene load (tick 5-9 ms) AND the new scene's first draw (4-9 ms) together; under a fully closed iris nothing of the scene is visible, and the ~45 frames a door waits and its iris closes are idle.
experiments.method: perf-rig door frames (f75-f97) on 5 worlds, develop vs change, each run twice in one session; under a closed iris only the iris disc is drawn; the next environment's shape paths are built during the wait in ≤1 ms slices (StageController.upcomingBlueprints); lazy backdrop chunks also pre-record the unseen chunks nearest the view in ≤0.5 ms a frame; skia-parity over 7 worlds x 6 camera positions; doorWarmup.test red with either part removed.
experiments.before: door frame 9-17 ms (load and first draw in one frame)
experiments.after: load frame 4.4-8 ms with ~0.03 ms draw; first draw on the next frame 5.7-10.7 ms: worst single door frame about a third lower
experiments.evidence: skia-parity: 0 differing channels (42 camera positions); doorWarmup.test.ts. Develop had independently landed lazy chunk recording (EXP-021), so the gain is the iris skip + path warm-up + look-ahead only.
